This is asset-copilot, an evaluated assistant for commercial real estate portfolio analysis. Everything here runs on synthetic data. The home page shows a live snapshot of the portfolio: sixty properties, about four hundred and sixty active leases, and this month's revenue, expenses and N O I against budget.
Let's start with a sample question: which five cities have the most properties?
The agent writes a read-only database query, runs it, and checks its own answer. That usually takes a few seconds.
The answer comes first. Underneath, it says whether every number was traced back to a cited source.
Sources are one click away. This is the exact query that ran, and the tables it read. The agent cannot change the data.
Now a question that needs both the documents and the database: what base rent does a lease abstract state, and does it match our records?
This one searches the lease documents as well as running a query, and compares the two.
The answer says what the document states and what the database holds, and flags any difference instead of quietly picking one.
The source cards show the query, and the passage from the lease abstract that was cited, with its page.
One click records a thumbs up. Ratings and notes are saved, so they can become new test questions later.
It also knows what it cannot do. Asked to forecast next year's N O I, it declines and explains why, rather than guessing.
The view switch changes presentation, never the answer. In the analyst view, sources open by default and show run details.
The variance report compares actuals to budget. Every number is computed in code, not by the model. Flagged items come first, largest first.
The commentary is drafted by the model, then checked automatically: any number that is not in the tables is rejected.
Selecting a flag shows that property over recent months, and one click opens its full report.

The agent is measured with an evaluation set of one hundred and forty-six questions, and passes all of them. But I wrote those questions myself, so they catch regressions rather than prove quality. The next step is questions from other people, and repeated runs to measure noise.
While it works, the agent is searching the lease documents and running a read-only database query. Every step is written to an audit log.
Before it answers, every number in the draft has to appear in one of those results. If one does not, the answer is marked as not fully verified.
The report has two parts. First, the numbers, calculated directly from the database. Then the model drafts the commentary, which is checked against those numbers.
Opening the full report asks for just this property: its own numbers, its own flags, and its own commentary.
The model is writing and checking the commentary for this property now. It takes a few seconds.
Here is the single property report. The headline numbers and the flagged item match the row we selected.
Selecting a flag also pulls the three earlier months for that property, so you can see whether this is a one-off or a trend.
Back on the home page, the snapshot refreshes from the same read-only service.
